I gave Codex and GPT-6 Astra $10,000 of real money to trade stocks for seven trading days, and the goal was to beat the S&P 500. 

You'll see how I set up the routines and agent handoffs, why I had to hand the actual trades to a Grok Bot, and how I changed the strategy when the agent was trading too cautiously. I check in at the end of every trading day with the actual numbers, including the day six Fed rate hike that dragged the portfolio down.

Viewers should be careful about treating this video as evidence that AI can trade profitably. By the creator’s own figures, the account finished at $9,900 versus $9,980 for the S&P 500: a 1% loss and 0.8 percentage points of underperformance.
Throughout the challenge, he repeatedly pushes the system to trade more, removes filters, and increases exposure because he is frustrated with inactivity. Saying he would rather lose $500 than see little activity is a major red flag. More trades and less cash do not mean better decisions.
With frequent human interventions, changing rules, and only seven trading days, this experiment cannot establish a reliable trading edge. Screenshots alone also do n
The biggest takeaway for me: the AI wasn’t really trading alone. Nate was constantly adjusting its strategy. That changes the experiment a lot.

What stood out wasn’t whether Astra beat the S&P — it was how much its behavior changed once the human started pushing it to take more risk. At D2C, that raises a more interesting question: when an autonomous agent makes the trades but humans still define the objective and risk tolerance, who is actually making the decision?
